name: Applied kinesiology

card.summary: A muscle-testing system from chiropractic that practitioners use to pick supplements and diets, which people turn to in the hope of improving health, physique and appearance.
card.aka: AK, muscle testing, manual muscle testing (AK style)
card.note: Allergy and medical bodies advise against using it to diagnose conditions or choose foods; it can lead to unnecessary elimination diets.

quick.overview:
Applied kinesiology (AK) is a system in which a practitioner presses on a patient's outstretched limb and judges whether a muscle 'holds' or 'gives'. Practitioners read the response as a sign of how well an organ, nutrient or emotional state is functioning. In looksmaxxing and wellness circles it appears as a way to decide which supplements, foods or posture-related treatments to use, with the aim of better skin, hair, body composition or posture.

The method was developed by Detroit chiropractor George Goodheart in 1964 and is taught through the International College of Applied Kinesiology. Published research has examined whether the muscle test gives consistent results and whether it can identify nutrient needs or food reactions; reviews by allergy and chiropractic researchers describe mostly negative or inconsistent findings.
quick.how: In a session the practitioner has the person hold an arm or leg in position, applies light pressure, and notes the response. A 'challenge' such as holding a supplement, touching a body area or thinking of a food is added and the test repeated; a change in the response is interpreted as a sign of need or intolerance. The result is then used to suggest supplements, dietary changes, adjustments or acupressure. Some people also run informal muscle tests on themselves or friends at home.
quick.risks: The method itself is non-invasive. The risks reported in the medical literature are indirect: allergy reviews warn that AK-guided food testing may lead to unnecessary elimination diets, and that a missed real condition may go undiagnosed. Allergy societies and the American Cancer Society state that it should not be used to diagnose or treat illness.

lead: Applied kinesiology (AK) is a diagnostic and treatment system that uses manual muscle testing. A practitioner, typically a chiropractor, applies pressure to a limb the patient holds in position and judges whether the muscle resists or gives way; the response is taken to reveal the state of related organs, nutrition or emotional balance [1][8]. It should not be confused with kinesiology, the academic study of human movement.

In appearance-minded communities AK is encountered mainly as a way to personalise choices: which supplements to take for skin, hair or energy, which foods to avoid, or which structural adjustments to make for posture and the jaw. The chain proponents describe runs from 'finding what the body needs' to better health, which they expect to show in skin, physique and posture. This is how practitioners present it rather than an outcome shown in trials.

AK was introduced in 1964 by George Goodheart and is organised through the International College of Applied Kinesiology (ICAK) [8]. Research has examined the reliability of the muscle test and its use in food-allergy, nutrient and dental assessment. Systematic and narrative reviews describe mixed reliability findings and conclude that diagnostic claims are not supported by published studies [2][3][4][5][6].

angle.text: Practitioners use the muscle test to choose which supplements and foods to use and which structural treatments to apply, with the stated goal of improving overall health and, by extension, how a person looks and carries themselves. Followers describe it as individualised guidance; the link to appearance outcomes is as claimed by practitioners.

paras: Applied kinesiology holds that each organ is linked to a specific muscle, so that a change in that muscle's response reflects a problem with the organ. Mainstream medicine does not share this 'viscerosomatic' premise, and Wikipedia notes it as a core AK idea [8]. The practitioner judges the strength of the response subjectively, often with the arm held out and pressed down [8][7].

Several variants are used. In nutrient or allergen testing, the patient holds or touches a substance and the test is repeated; a change in response is read as the substance helping or harming. In 'therapy localization', the patient's hand is placed over a body area and a change in muscle response is read as a sign that area needs treatment [8]. Goodheart's system draws on chiropractic, osteopathic reflex points and acupuncture meridian ideas [1]. Treatments that follow can include adjustments, acupressure, nutrition advice and supplements [1].

Goodheart began developing the approach in 1964 and taught it to other chiropractors; a study group formed in 1973 and became the ICAK, which named itself in 1974 and certified charter members in 1976 [8]. A 2003 survey cited by Wikipedia found AK was the tenth most used chiropractic technique in the United States, used by 37.6 percent of chiropractors [8].

Beyond chiropractic, muscle testing has spread among naturopaths, nutritionists and wellness practitioners, and is the basis of home 'muscle test' methods for checking supplements or foods. Applied kinesiology is also sometimes confused with kinesiology taping and with sports kinesiology degrees, which are unrelated to it.

sections.h: Use for supplements, diet and appearance
paras: In the supplement and diet setting, practitioners say the muscle test shows whether a particular nutrient, food or product suits the individual. Proponents say this helps them target deficiencies behind poor skin, hair loss, low energy or difficulty building muscle. Forum users who discuss it in the context of training and chiropractic care describe encountering the 'applied kinesiology' label on a practitioner's credentials and expecting something different [10].

Dentistry and jaw research is one area where AK has been applied to facial structure. A narrative review identified a small number of AK studies on temporomandibular disorders and dental materials, and noted that an association between bite relationships and muscle strength had been observed in the literature [5].

A 2025 systematic review of manual muscle testing within AK found seven eligible studies; four were of good or very good quality and three were poor or inadequate. Within-examiner reliability was high in one study and poor in two, so reliability results were inconsistent [2]. A broader literature review of manual muscle testing found a body of research going back to 1915 and discussed its reliability and validity in clinical use [11].

For food allergy, reviews by allergy specialists list AK among unproven diagnostic tests. One review says such tests lack standardisation and reproducibility and that blinded controlled studies had not supported them [3][4][7]. A 2005 double-blind study of dental material testing with AK was also published in the Journal of Dental Research [9]. A 1988 double-blind study reported by Wikipedia found AK nutrient assessment no more useful than random guessing, while a 1998 pilot study reported that most food sensitivities identified by AK matched serum tests; Wikipedia presents the overall literature as not supporting diagnostic use [8].

The American Cancer Society states that scientific evidence does not support the claim that AK can diagnose or treat cancer or other illness. Allergy organisations including the AAAAI, EAACI and the World Allergy Organization advise against using it to diagnose allergy, and a 2015 Australian government review placed it among therapies with no clear evidence of effectiveness [8]. The Danish Chiropractic Association stated in 1998 that AK is not a form of chiropractic care [8]. Skeptical commentators attribute the observed responses to the ideomotor effect, unconscious small movements [8]. Practitioners and the ICAK maintain that the method is a clinical tool used by trained professionals and point to studies reporting reliability and neurological rationale [1].

The reported concerns are indirect. Allergy reviews say AK and similar unconventional tests may lead to unnecessary elimination diets, and that medical conditions can go unaddressed when a muscle test substitutes for standard assessment [3][6].

timeline.event: George Goodheart begins developing applied kinesiology in Detroit [8]

lore.intro: In training and wellness communities, AK is usually met through a chiropractor or naturopath who uses muscle testing to recommend supplements. It also appears in fitness forum threads where members discuss practitioners' credentials [10].

claims.claim: A muscle test can show which supplements your body needs
claims.believers: Practitioners say holding a supplement while a limb is tested shows whether it strengthens or weakens the body, and use this to personalise supplement stacks [1].
claims.experts: A 1988 double-blind study found AK nutrient assessment no more useful than random guessing, and allergy reviews list it as unproven [8][6].

claims.claim: Muscle testing can reveal food allergies or intolerances
claims.believers: Proponents say a change in muscle response when a food is touched or held identifies sensitivities, including those found in a small 1998 pilot comparison with serum tests [8].
claims.experts: Allergy societies advise against it and reviews describe a lack of reproducibility and correlation with disease [3][4][6].

claims.claim: Muscle weakness can show structural problems that affect posture and the jaw
claims.believers: AK practitioners say muscle responses point to structural imbalances that can be treated with adjustments or reflex work [1].
claims.experts: A review of AK in dentistry found only a couple of studies and said the diagnostic and treatment claims are not supported, though bite and muscle strength associations have been noted [5].

claims.claim: The test results are reproducible between practitioners
claims.believers: ICAK-aligned authors point to studies with high reliability for specific tests [2].
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review found reliability varied, high in one study and poor in two [2].
